findings.suggested_fix: Replace return None in the OSError handler with if index == attempts - 1: raise, allowing earlier failures to continue the loop.
findings.why_it_matters: Existing callers requesting multiple attempts now receive None after the first OSError, even when a subsequent call would succeed. Exhausted failures also stop propagating, changing the public failure contract into an indistinguishable success-shaped sentinel. Restoring retry continuation and re-raising on the final attempt preserves both established behaviors.

findings.title: First OSError bypasses retries and failure propagation
findings.suggested_fix: Replace return None in the OSError handler with if index == attempts - 1: raise; allow earlier failures to continue the loop.
findings.why_it_matters: A transient source failure returns None after one call, so load(source) never reaches a successful retry despite requesting three attempts. Persistent failures likewise return None instead of propagating the last OSError, hiding the failure from callers. Restoring the final-attempt raise preserves both bounded retries and failure propagation.

caller.py:4:     return fetch(source, 3)

app.py:2:     for index in range(attempts):
Executed transient source with attempts=3: returned None after one call instead of succeeding on call two; always-failing source returned None after one call instead of raising on call three.

findings.title: Failed delivery discards the first queued item
findings.suggested_fix: Use item = queue[0], call send(item), then call queue.pop(0) only after send returns successfully.
findings.why_it_matters: When send raises, the first queued item has already been removed and cannot be retried. For queue [1, 2], a failed send of 1 leaves [2], violating the required failure behavior. Reading the first item before sending and removing it only after success preserves the queue on failure.
evidence: app.py:10:     item = queue.pop(0)
app.py:11:     send(item)
Executed deliver([1, 2], send) with send raising OSError: the exception propagated but the queue became [2].
Executed deliver([1, 2], failed_send) where failed_send raises OSError: exception propagated but queue became [2].
Trigger: queue is ['first', 'second'] and send raises OSError before delivery. app.py:10 removes 'first' before app.py:11 calls send(item).
Path: OSError propagates from send; there is no restoration of the removed item, leaving ['second']. A caller that retries deliver(queue, send) now selects 'second'.

Outcome: an inline reproduction produced queue_after_failure: ['second'], retry_sent: ['second'], remaining_queue: []; the first item was never delivered. This violates R3 and makes retry delivery skip FIFO work.
